title: Middle East Airlines 438
summary: Middle East Airlines Flight 438, a Boeing 720 with 81 aboard, was destroyed by a bomb in flight at 11,300 feet on January 1, 1976, while en route from Beirut to Dubai via Abu Dhabi. The bomb was planted in the cargo hold by Omani militants with a timer set to explode after landing in Muscat. Flight delays from boarding and baggage loading caused the bomb to detonate in flight. The aircraft broke up and crashed 37 kilometers northwest of Qaisumah, Saudi Arabia.

title: Aeroflot 2003
summary: Aeroflot Flight 2003 crashed on January 3, 1976, while operating a Tupolev Tu-124V from Moscow-Vnukovo Airport on a domestic flight to Brest, Belarus with an intermediate stop in Minsk. During initial climb-out after takeoff, as the aircraft entered clouds, both artificial horizons failed for unknown reasons, leaving the crew with no visual reference. The pilots became spatially disoriented and lost control of the aircraft. The Tu-124V banked steeply to the left, entered a dive, and crashed into a house 7 kilometers from Vnukovo International Airport, killing all 61 people on board and 1 person on the ground.

title: Aeroflot 3739 (1976)
summary: Aeroflot Flight 3739, a Tupolev Tu-104A, crashed during takeoff from Irkutsk on February 9, 1976. The aircraft began rolling to the right at 300 km/h rotation speed, forcing pilots to roll it 20 degrees left. Calculations showed the right fuel tanks held 1,300-1,500 kg more fuel than the left, creating asymmetric weight. The pilots' aileron inputs were inadequate; the proper response would have been to reduce throttle sharply. The aircraft became uncontrollable at 30 m altitude and crashed 180 m past the runway end at a 70° bank angle, killing 24 of 114 aboard.

title: Alaska Airlines 60
summary: Flight 60 departed Juneau and established an ILS approach to Ketchikan under low cloud ceilings and low visibility due to light snow and fog. The captain abandoned the precision approach for a visual approach at 1000 ft altitude. The aircraft touched down long at 145 knots alongside a tailwind of 3 knots on the wet runway with poor braking. The captain initiated a go-around but the thrust reverser mechanism failed to fully disengage, preventing full takeoff thrust. The aircraft overran the runway and struck an antenna array support in a ravine.

title: ČSA 001
summary: A Czechoslovak Airlines Ilyushin Il-18B crashed into Zlaté Piesky Lake on final approach to Bratislava on 28 July 1976, killing 76 of the 79 people on board. The crew executed a highly unstabilized ILS approach with excessive descent rates of 4,320 feet per minute instead of the normal 10 meters per second, variable speeds, and improper flap configuration changes. title: 1976 Anapa mid-air collision
summary: On 9 September 1976, an Antonov An-24RV (Aeroflot Flight 7957, 47 passengers and 5 crew) and a Yakovlev Yak-40 (Aeroflot Flight S-31, 14 passengers and 4 crew) collided in mid-air at 5700 meters altitude off the coast of Anapa in the Soviet Union. The primary cause was an air traffic controller error: the controller failed to instruct the Yak-40 to change altitude after it passed through certain waypoints, resulting in both aircraft remaining at the same 5700-meter altitude. Contributing factors included failure of both crews to remain sufficiently alert and lack of appropriate situational analysis. All 70 people on both aircraft were killed. Both aircraft broke apart and fell into the Black Sea.

It was discovered that Flight 830 had flown into a mountain at a height of 4625 ft near the village of Servia.
Aircraft disintegrated over the next 200 metres before becoming shortly airborne again, finally crashing at the foot of another hill.

title: Aeroflot 2415
summary: A Tupolev Tu-104B crashed shortly after takeoff from Moscow-Sheremetyevo in bad weather with visibility limited to 1,500 meters. After a safe takeoff and banking right to a heading of 265 degrees, the aircraft continued to bank to the right uncontrollably, losing altitude and picking up speed in a steep dive. The aircraft crashed 9.5 kilometers from the airport, exploding on impact. The State Supervisory Commission found failure of the artificial horizon contributed to crew disorientation combined with poor visibility and lack of warning indications.
probable_cause: Failure of the artificial horizon led to crew disorientation. In poor visibility and without warnings of the artificial horizon failure, the crew could not recover when the aircraft entered a steep right-turning dive. The crew performed excellently under the circumstances but lacked correct data about the aircraft's attitude.

title: Aeroflot 36 (1976)
summary: An Antonov An-24 on approach to Kyiv airport crashed on 17 December 1976 in deteriorating visibility. The airport's instrument landing system was out of service for maintenance. Weather visibility had dropped below the 700-meter minimum for the An-24, but the aero-meteorological station did not detect this drop and did not warn air traffic control. ATC provided ambiguous commands and did not guide the flight by landing radar. The aircraft descended below the published glide path without warning, started descending too late with excessive vertical velocity, and did not see runway lights at critical height but continued approach, resulting in 48 fatalities.
probable_cause: Inadequate weather monitoring and ATC guidance during approach in weather below minimum limits, combined with ILS unavailability and inadequate danger height alarm system.

title: EgyptAir 864
summary: EgyptAir Flight 864, a Boeing 707, crashed into a weaving mill in Bangkok at 03:45 local time while approaching Runway 21L. All 52 on board were killed. The investigation found pilot error in descending below minimum altitude without proper monitoring, combined with inadequate weather information from ATC regarding visibility of only 4,000 m with low clouds.
probable_cause: Pilot error in descending below the minimum altitude for which the flight had received clearance without adequate ground references. Contributing fault was assigned to ATC and the dispatcher for providing an inappropriate clearance.
